articleTitle: Installation of electrical equipment for flue gas desulphurisation retrofit at Drax power station
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrical Aspects of Desulphurisation
abstract: Installation of flue gas desulphurisation plant at existing power stations inevitably clashes with existing services, which requires their relocation and diversion. The Drax FGD installation has highlighted the extent of this. The author discusses the diversion and location of electrical equipment caused by the retrofit at Drax. The diversions include a 400 kV overhead line, a cable tunnel, and fuel oil and propane systems. The location of the electrical supplies, switchgear and auxiliary transformers are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical supplies for flue gas desulphurisation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrical Aspects of Desulphurisation
abstract: In 1987, in order to reduce the sulphur emissions from fossil-fired power stations, approval was given for the installation of FGD using the limestone-gypsum process on units 4, 5 and 6 at Drax. The author considers the electrical system design aspects of this retrofit project. This includes a description of the main design objectives and constraints on the retrofit project. The author discusses the supply sources, which come from either generator output or a separate grid source, the loads, the selection of voltages, and the transformers and switchgear.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control and instrumentation aspects of flue gas desulphurisation (FGD)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electrical Aspects of Desulphurisation
abstract: The author concentrates on the control and instrumentation aspects of FGD as retrofitted to a 4*500 MW coal fired power station using the limestone/gypsum process. The author describes the process and the associated equipment. The parameters to be monitored and controlled are listed. The control positions for each process are discussed and the use of a SCADA system described. The chemical monitoring instrumentation is also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
